narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average ranking of about 5.8 among students who were admitted, signaling that your later-year performance lagged behind most successful applicants. Your LSAT score of 20 was the second most important factor; this is far below the average of 37 among accepted students and strongly increased the model’s estimate of failure risk. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.7 worked in the opposite direction, modestly lowering the predicted risk of failure, yet it was not enough to offset the other two factors.

Taken together, the model saw your lower third-year ranking and LSAT performance as clear indicators that the first-time bar passage would be difficult, leading directly to the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, while also working to improve your class ranking in the remaining law school years. These improvements would meaningfully change how a similar model would evaluate your future applications. (218 words)
